expansion:
A is right. Complete ptosis, a “down and out” eye, diplopia, and a fixed dilated pupil indicate a complete third-nerve palsy with pupil involvement. The lecture identifies “ptosis + ‘down and out’ + a dilated pupil” as “a complete third nerve palsy with pupil involvement” (L30, slide 12). It further labels pupil involvement as “Compression” and illustrates a posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing the superficial pupillary fibres, producing “pupillary dilation” (L30, slide 13). Sudden severe unilateral headache with this pupil-involving palsy therefore requires urgent cerebrovascular imaging with CTA to identify an aneurysm (not taken from the course material). The lecture does not specify an investigation for nerve palsy, stating that CT, MRI, and angiography are not mentioned (L30, slide 13).

B is wrong because fasting blood glucose may help assess diabetes as a vascular risk factor, but it is not the urgent test for this presentation. The lecture contrasts vascular disease causing central nerve-fibre infarction, in which the “pupil normal,” with external aneurysmal compression causing pupillary dilation (L30, slide 13). This patient has a dilated, nonreactive pupil, fitting compression rather than the pupil-spared vascular pattern.

C is wrong because a tension test does not investigate a third-nerve palsy or exclude a compressive intracranial aneurysm (not taken from the course material).

D is wrong because orbital CT is aimed at orbital pathology and does not provide the required dedicated assessment of the cerebral circulation for a suspected posterior communicating artery aneurysm. CTA is the urgent vascular study in this clinical context (not taken from the course material).
objective: A painful pupil-involving complete third-nerve palsy requires urgent cerebrovascular imaging for a compressive aneurysm.
